editorial.headline: Conventional Re-Guaranteeing: Open Nationally, Clear in Bali
editorial.standfirst: A precise guarantee activity, open to full foreign ownership nationally and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium, centred on guarantee companies’ financial obligations.
editorial.body:
Conventional re-guaranteeing is a specialised financial-guarantee activity. It consists of providing guarantees for the fulfilment of guarantee companies’ financial obligations, undertaken through conventional arrangements. That is the centre of this classification: a re-guarantee business conducted conventionally, with its guarantee directed to the financial obligations of guarantee companies. The scope gives the activity both a precise commercial subject and a precise obligation. It is best understood from that stated relationship, rather than by treating the word “guarantee” as a catch-all. In registration terms, the description points to the guarantee operation itself and to the companies whose financial commitments it addresses.

Who can register it is unusually broad on scale. The record opens the activity to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar enterprises—micro, small, medium and large. The scale field therefore does not confine this activity to one end of the business-size spectrum. Yet scale is not a substitute for scope: whether the enterprise is micro or large, the recorded activity remains conventional re-guaranteeing, and the recorded service remains a guarantee for meeting guarantee companies’ financial obligations. Reading the two fields together keeps the registration question grounded: broad scale eligibility, but a tightly stated business function.

Nationally, the foreign-investment stance is clear-cut. The activity is marked TERBUKA, or open, and its maximum foreign ownership is 100 percent. For a foreign investor, that records a national path to full ownership of an enterprise carrying out this stated activity. There is no need to dilute that point: the maximum shown in the record is 100 percent. The listed scale availability and the foreign-ownership ceiling answer different questions, but together they establish a clear national position for this defined conventional re-guaranteeing business.

Bali calls for an equally exact reading. The provincial status is OK_or_HIGHER_RISK, and the record says the activity is not blocked by the moratorium. Its stated reason is that, at the Besar scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi: medium-high/high. The Bali rule cited in the record permanently blocks PMA registration, island-wide, for Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI activities. This activity is not placed in that blocked group. The honest Bali conclusion is clean: a foreign investor is not barred from registering this activity in Bali by that moratorium. That conclusion does not alter the national ownership figure; it confirms that Bali’s recorded treatment introduces no separate block here.
editorial.pullQuote: Open to full foreign ownership nationally, this activity is also not barred in Bali by the recorded moratorium.
